messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Akua had always been a self-sufficient person, able to fix anything with her hands and face any challenge head-on. As a plumber, she took pride in being one of the few women in a male-dominated field. But it was this very independence that made her recent struggles all the more difficult to accept. Growing up, Akua had suffered at the hands of an abusive caregiver. The memories of those events were etched into her mind like scars on her skin. She tried not to think about them, but certain sounds – the creaking of a door, the rustling of fabric – would transport her back to that time and place. Hearing names similar to her abuser's or catching a glimpse of someone with a similar voice tone would send her spiraling into anxiety. Akua had come to believe that she was somehow to blame for what happened to her as a child. "If only I were stronger," she would tell herself, "if only I were more worthy." This self-doubt seeped into every aspect of her life. She felt like there was something fundamentally wrong with her, that she was defective in some way. Even the work she loved – fixing pipes and unclogging drains – no longer brought her joy. As a result, Akua began to avoid anything that reminded her of her abuser or the traumatic events of her past. She stopped attending family gatherings where she might encounter people with similar names or voices. She avoided authority figures, including police officers and healthcare professionals, fearing they would judge her or see right through her facade. When working on a job site, she would become anxious if someone with a similar voice tone was nearby. But these avoidance behaviors only served to reinforce Akua's negative self-image. The more she withdrew from the world, the more convinced she became that she was unfixable, that nothing in her life had meaning anymore. She started to ruminate on all the ways others had wronged her – including her abuser, but also people who were simply trying to help. "Why did they do this to me?" she would ask herself, getting lost in a cycle of resentment and self-pity. The consequences of these behaviors began to accumulate. Akua's relationships with her loved ones started to fray, as she became increasingly isolated and withdrawn. Her work suffered too – she was late to job sites, or would leave early, unable to shake off the feeling of unease that lingered long after she'd left a particular location. One day, while working on a particularly difficult plumbing job, Akua's anxiety became overwhelming. She had to take a break, stepping outside into the fresh air to calm herself down. It was then that she realized she couldn't keep living like this – constantly avoiding triggers, stuck in a cycle of self-blame and resentment. Something inside her shifted, and for the first time in years, Akua felt a spark of hope. Maybe, just maybe, it was time to confront her demons head-on, rather than running from them. With a newfound sense of determination, Akua made an appointment with a therapist, hoping to finally break free from the grip of her past and find meaning in her life once more.
